articles.title: The Slave Trader Who Wrote the Hymn
articles.dek: A man who cursed God on the deck of a slave ship became the author of the world's most-sung song about grace. Paul knew exactly how that happens.
articles.quote: God didn't just forgive Paul's worst chapter. He made it Exhibit A of his patience.
articles.body:
On the night of March 21, 1748, a ship called the Greyhound was taking on water in the middle of the North Atlantic. Waves broke over the deck. The hull groaned like it was about to split. Down in the hold, a young ship's mate named John Newton tied himself to the pump and bailed for his life, certain he was about to drown.

Newton was not a good man. He cursed God for sport. He mocked other sailors who prayed. He had already spent years in the slave trade, a business he would later call a trade in human misery, and he carried himself with the swagger of someone who answered to no one. But that night, exhausted, soaked, and out of options, he heard himself say something he never expected: Lord, have mercy on us. The ship barely survived. Newton always marked that date afterward as the night everything in him started to turn.

It wasn't instant. He stayed in the slave trade for several more years before his conscience finally caught up with his prayer. But eventually he left the sea, became a pastor, and in 1772 wrote a hymn that begins, "Amazing grace, how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me." Filipinos have sung it at funerals, at baptisms, even at karaoke nights, for generations — most without knowing the man who wrote it once bought and sold people like cargo.

Paul tells almost the same story about himself, and he tells it with the same bluntness Newton used. Writing to Timothy, the young pastor he's mentoring in Ephesus, Paul doesn't dress up his past. He doesn't say "I made some mistakes" or "I had a complicated journey." He names it plainly.

Before he was an apostle, Paul hunted Christians. He approved of their executions. He dragged believers — men and women — out of their homes and into prison, convinced he was serving God the whole time. Then, on the road to Damascus, a light stopped him in his tracks and a voice asked why he was persecuting it. He went from the church's most feared enemy to its most relentless missionary, and by the time he writes this letter, decades later, he still can't quite get over it.

"Even though I was once a blasphemer and a persecutor and a violent man," he writes, "I was shown mercy because I acted in ignorance and unbelief" (1 Timothy 1:13). Then he says something that stops you cold if you slow down to read it.

"Here is a trustworthy saying that deserves full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners—of whom I am the worst. But for that very reason I was shown mercy so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display his immense patience as an example for those who would believe in him and receive eternal life." (1 Timothy 1:15–16)

Read that twice. Paul isn't just saying God forgave him and moved on, the way you might wipe a slate clean and never mention it again. He's saying God used him — specifically the worst version of him — on purpose. "For that very reason," he writes. Not despite his record. Because of it. His sin became the material God chose to put his patience on display, so that anyone reading Paul's story afterward would think, if God's mercy stretched that far for him, it can stretch far enough for me.

That's worth sitting with, because most of us handle our worst chapters the opposite way. We file them away. We hope no one asks. We let shame convince us that the only useful thing to do with our failures is to bury them deep enough that they stop defining us. Paul does something almost scandalous by comparison — he puts his failure in a letter that would be read aloud in churches, copied by hand, and preserved for two thousand years, because he's convinced that his rescue is actually good news for someone else's rescue.

Newton understood this instinctively, even if he didn't know he was echoing an apostle. He didn't erase his past once he became a pastor. He kept a written account of his years at sea, the storm, the slow unraveling of his old life, and he let people read it. He later became a quiet but steady encourager to a young member of Parliament named William Wilberforce, who was wrestling with whether to leave politics for the ministry. Newton told him to stay exactly where he was and use his position to fight the slave trade from the inside. Wilberforce did. It took him decades, but in 1807 the British Parliament finally abolished the slave trade — and the old sea captain who once profited from it lived just long enough to see it happen.

Notice what that means. Newton's worst chapter didn't just get forgiven in private. It became part of the very story that helped end a horror he'd once participated in. His mercy had a ripple.

This is the fresh angle worth carrying out of 1 Timothy 1: your worst season is not a liability God is managing around. If you've surrendered it to him, it may be the very thing he intends to use — not because the sin was good, but because the mercy that met it is too good to keep quiet. Paul doesn't call himself "the worst of sinners" to wallow. He says it so that the next person drowning in guilt has somewhere to look and see that the door is wider than they thought.

So here's something to do with your own hardest chapter today: stop asking only how do I move past this, and start asking who might need to hear that God met me here. You don't need a pulpit or a hymn. You need one honest sentence to one person who's convinced they've gone too far. Tell them what Paul told Timothy — mercy reached you, specifically, in the exact spot you thought was unreachable. That sentence might be the storm that turns someone else's ship around.

articles.title: The Gathering Comes First
articles.dek: When Judah's leaders scattered the flock, God didn't wait for better management before he started bringing people home — a quiet street corner in Quezon City shows what that looks like in practice.
articles.quote: God didn't wait for better shepherds before he started gathering the sheep — and neither should we.
articles.body:
In April 2021, on a quiet side street in Quezon City called Maginhawa, a woman named Ana Patricia Non rolled a small wooden cart out to the edge of the road. She hung a cardboard sign on it, handwritten in Filipino: Magbigay ayon sa kakayahan, kumuha batay sa pangangailangan — give what you can, take what you need. There was no guard posted beside it. No logbook, no ID checks, no one keeping score. Just rice, canned goods, a few eggs, some vegetables, laid out for whoever needed them, refilled by whoever had extra. By the next morning the cart was empty. By noon it was full again. Within weeks, thousands of copycat pantries had appeared on sidewalks and street corners all over the country, every one of them running on the same quiet logic: when a season turns hard and people start to scatter, somebody has to start gathering them back.

Jeremiah 23 opens with God saying almost exactly that — except the people doing the scattering were the ones who were supposed to be gathering. "Shepherd" was the standard word for a king in the ancient world, long before anyone thought of Jesus holding a lamb. Judah had been passed through a string of shepherd-kings who did everything but shepherd. They taxed the flock to fund their own comfort. They ignored the poor. They courted foreign alliances instead of listening to the prophets God kept sending. By the time Jeremiah wrote this chapter, Babylon's armies were already a shadow on the horizon, and the flock of Judah was starting to scatter in fear — some into exile, some into hiding, some simply lost.

God's anger lands first, and it is not soft: "Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!" declares the LORD (Jeremiah 23:1). It's the kind of line you'd expect a chapter about betrayed leadership to end on. Instead, it's where the real story begins.

"I myself will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them and will bring them back to their pasture, where they will be fruitful and increase in number. I will place shepherds over them who will tend them, and they will no longer be afraid or terrified, nor will any be missing," declares the LORD. (Jeremiah 23:3–4)

Read that again slowly, and notice the order. God doesn't say, "First I'll find better leaders, and once they're in place, the flock will be gathered." He says the opposite. The gathering comes first. "I myself will gather" is verse 3. "I will place shepherds over them" is verse 4. Before a single new leader is appointed, before any structure is rebuilt, before Judah has a king worth following again, God is already out walking the hillsides, already calling the sheep home by name.

That's worth sitting with, because most of us quietly wait for the opposite order. We assume nothing good can be gathered until the system is fixed — until the right people are finally in charge, until the institution earns back our trust, until someone with the proper title steps up. Jeremiah 23 suggests God doesn't operate that way. The gathering doesn't wait on the org chart. It starts the moment someone — anyone — is willing to do it.

Ana Patricia Non wasn't a shepherd by any title. She had no office, no staff, no budget line. She was twenty-six years old with a cart and a sign. But in the spirit of verse 3, she did the one thing shepherds exist to do: she made sure that in her small corner of the city, during a season when a lot of people felt forgotten, nobody went missing. That's the phrase that closes God's promise — "nor will any be missing." Not nor will any go hungry, though that's true too. Nor will any be missing. The ache behind the whole chapter isn't really about bread. It's about being counted, noticed, kept track of by someone who actually cares whether you made it home.

Jeremiah doesn't stop at a promise of better management, either. Two verses later, the chapter does something no human government could ever pull off on its own: "The days are coming," declares the LORD, "when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, a King who will reign wisely and do what is just and right in the land... This is the name by which he will be called: The LORD Our Righteous Savior" (Jeremiah 23:5–6). The fix for bad shepherding was never going to be no shepherds. It was one true Shepherd — righteous enough to define, for every leader who came after him, what good shepherding actually looks like. Christians have long read this as a straight line toward Jesus, who would later stand in front of crowds that Israel's leaders had left "harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd" (Matthew 9:36), and simply begin to teach them, heal them, feed them.

Here's the human wisdom tucked inside all of this, the kind Jeremiah's original readers would have needed just as much as we do: you don't need a title to practice verse 3. You need a willingness to gather. Most of us are not in charge of a nation, a company, or even a barangay. But all of us know someone who has gone a little quiet lately — stopped replying to messages, stopped showing up at the table, drifted a half-step further away each week without anyone quite noticing when it started. Scattering rarely announces itself. It just happens, person by person, until one day somebody realizes the usual group chat has gone silent, or a cousin hasn't been to a family gathering in over a year, or a coworker has started eating lunch alone.

God's answer to a scattered flock was never a memo. It was presence — "I myself will gather." That's the model worth copying, whether you lead a household, a team at work, a small group at church, or nothing official at all. You don't have to fix the whole system to gather one person back. You just have to be willing to be the one who goes looking.

God didn't wait for better shepherds before he started gathering the sheep — and neither should we.

So here's something to do this week, small enough to actually finish: think of one person who has quietly gone missing from your circle. Not someone in crisis, necessarily — just someone who has drifted. Send the message. Save them a seat. Leave the extra plate. No cart required, no sign, no permission slip. Just the oldest instinct in Jeremiah 23, the one God claims for himself first: go gather what has scattered, and make sure nobody on your watch stays missing.

articles.title: Low Enough to Lift You
articles.dek: Psalm 113 says God is enthroned above the heavens — and still bends down low enough to touch the dust. One priest's choice to live among the outcasts shows what that kind of glory looks like up close.
articles.quote: His glory isn't measured by how high his throne sits. It's measured by how low he's willing to bend to reach you.
articles.body:
In 1873, a Belgian priest named Jozef De Veuster stepped off a small boat onto a strip of black lava rock on the island of Molokai, Hawaii. The place was called Kalaupapa, and it was a place people were sent to disappear. Anyone diagnosed with leprosy — what we now call Hansen's disease — was forcibly removed from their family, loaded onto a ship, and left on that isolated peninsula to die. There were no doctors there. No real shelter. Just a few thousand people the rest of the world had decided to stop looking at.

De Veuster, known to history as Father Damien, didn't come to visit. He came to stay. He ate from the same bowls the patients used. He dressed wounds with his bare hands when no one else would. He built houses, dug graves, and buried the dead himself when there was no one left able to carry a coffin. He learned their songs. For sixteen years he lived inside a community that medicine had given up on — until one Sunday morning, he stood to address the congregation and began, for the first time, with different words: "We lepers." He had contracted the disease himself. He died among them in 1889, by then simply one of them.

Nobody made Damien go lower. He chose it. And it's worth holding that picture next to a very old song that Jewish families still sing at Passover — Psalm 113.

The psalm opens about as high as a song can open. "The LORD is exalted over all the nations, his glory above the heavens" (Ps 113:4). This is the loftiest possible language for God — a King seated far above every throne, every government, every galaxy. If the psalm stopped there, it would still be true, and still be worth singing. But it doesn't stop there. The very next line asks a question that answers itself: "Who is like the LORD our God, the One who sits enthroned on high, who stoops down to look on the heavens and the earth?" (Ps 113:5–6).

Read that again slowly. God is so high that he has to stoop down just to glance at the heavens — let alone the earth beneath them. And having bent down to look, he doesn't stay at a distance. He reaches.

He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap; he seats them with princes, with the princes of their people. He settles the childless woman in her home as a happy mother of children. Praise the LORD. (Psalm 113:7–9, NIV)

Notice what the psalm doesn't say. It doesn't say God is impressed by strength, or drawn to the people who already have a seat at the table. It names three very specific, very unglamorous addresses: the dust, the ash heap, and the empty house of a woman who has spent years waiting for a child she may never hold. These aren't metaphors for mild inconvenience. Sitting in ashes was what Job did when his whole life collapsed (Job 2:8). Dust was the floor beggars lay on at the city gate. A childless home, in that world, often meant a woman's future, security, and dignity all hinging on something she had no power to produce. These are rock-bottom places. And the psalm says this is precisely where God's reach is aimed.

Here's the turn worth sitting with: most songs praise God's greatness by pointing up — look how high, look how vast, look how far beyond us. This one proves his greatness by pointing down. The psalm doesn't separate the two. It puts "enthroned on high" and "stoops down" in the very same breath, as if the second phrase explains the first rather than contradicting it. His exaltation isn't despite the bending. The bending is what the exaltation is for. A throne that could only look at other thrones wouldn't be worth singing about. It's a throne that bends low enough to notice an ash heap that makes verse 4 worth anything at all.

That's what makes Damien's choice such an honest echo of this psalm rather than just a nice story next to it. He didn't lower his calling by moving into that colony. He fulfilled it. The descent wasn't a detour from his purpose — it was the clearest expression of it. Psalm 113 says the same thing about God himself: his glory isn't threatened by nearness to the dust. It's revealed by it.

His glory isn't measured by how high his throne sits. It's measured by how low he's willing to bend to reach you.

So where does that leave you this Monday? Maybe you're not on an ash heap in the dramatic sense — no collapsed life, no exile to a far island. But maybe there's a quieter version: a year of waiting for something that hasn't come, a room in your life that still feels empty, a week where you've felt more overlooked than seen. The psalm doesn't ask you to pretend the dust isn't dust. It tells you who already knows exactly where you're sitting, and that stooping down to that spot is not beneath him — it's where he's most himself.

And maybe it leaves you with a small, doable thing to carry today. Think of one person you've quietly filed under "beneath my attention" — not out of cruelty, just the ordinary blindness we all develop toward people who seem to have nothing to offer us. A kasambahay, a security guard, a relative everyone else has stopped calling. You don't need a boat to Molokai. You need one phone call, one five-minute visit, one moment of actually stooping down to look. That's the shape of the God we praise. It's worth becoming the shape of his people, too.

Praise the LORD — the one high enough to rule every nation, and low enough to lift you, personally, off the floor.

articles.title: Because It Was Him, Because It Was Me
articles.dek: A sixteenth-century friendship and an ancient proverb agree: the best friends were never chosen for a reason — and the truest ones never let go.
articles.quote: A thousand acquaintances can applaud a person. Only a friend stays when there is nothing left to applaud.
articles.body:
In 1558, at a crowded festival in Bordeaux, France, a young magistrate named Michel de Montaigne met another young magistrate named Étienne de La Boétie. They were, by any normal measure, strangers. But within a single evening, something happened between them that neither man could ever fully explain. Years later, when people asked Montaigne why he had loved La Boétie so completely, he gave an answer that has outlived both of them by nearly five centuries: “If you press me to say why I loved him, I feel this cannot be expressed, except by answering: because it was him, because it was me.”

Four years after that festival, La Boétie died of dysentery at thirty-two, with Montaigne at his bedside. Montaigne was undone. He eventually withdrew from public life to a tower on his family’s estate and began writing the short reflections that would help invent an entire literary form, the essay. The very first great one he wrote, the one that made the rest possible, he simply called “On Friendship.” He said that after La Boétie died, he only ever lived on afterward “as a shadow of himself.” People still quote that line today, because Montaigne put words to something most of us have felt but never managed to say out loud: some friendships are not just more of the same thing as ordinary acquaintance. They are a different kind of thing entirely. They do not multiply. They anchor.

That is the exact question Solomon is turning over at the very end of Proverbs 18. The chapter has already spent several verses on the power of the tongue — how words can nourish a life or starve it, heal it or wound it. Then, almost as a closing thought, comes a line about friendship that rewards slow reading.

One who has unreliable friends soon comes to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. (Proverbs 18:24, NIV)

Read it again and notice the shape of the sentence. The first half is plural — friends, companions, a whole crowd of them. The second half is singular — a friend. Solomon is making a quiet, almost mathematical observation: breadth and depth pull against each other. A person can collect companions by the dozen and still end up dangerously alone on the one night it matters. Or a person can have a single soul bound to theirs who never, ever leaves. The proverb is not telling us to distrust people or shrink our circles out of suspicion. It is simply telling the truth: quantity cannot buy what one loyal friend gives for free.

Here is something a first-time reader might miss. The Hebrew behind “sticks closer than a brother” uses the same root elsewhere translated “cling” — the word used for a husband and wife becoming one flesh. Solomon is not describing casual companionship. He is describing a bond with glue in it: the kind of friend who does not drift away when your circumstances change, your reputation takes a hit, or you simply stop being useful to know.

Most of us have tasted both halves of this verse. We have had seasons thick with people — invitations, group chats, a packed guest list for the birthday party — and then real trouble arrived, and the room emptied out fast. We have also, if we are fortunate, had the opposite: one person who showed up at the hospital, who answered the phone at two in the morning, who stayed exactly when staying cost them something. Solomon is not surprised by either experience. He is naming it so we stop being surprised by it too — and start investing differently.

But the proverb is doing more than offering practical advice about choosing friends wisely, true as that is. Read across the whole of Scripture, it is also quietly pointing forward. On the night before his death, Jesus sat with his closest companions and said something that reads like Proverbs 18:24 fulfilled in a person: “Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one’s life for one’s friends… I no longer call you servants… Instead, I have called you friends” (John 15:13–15). Montaigne loved La Boétie with everything in him, but it was La Boétie who died first, leaving Montaigne behind to grieve. Jesus reverses that entirely. He is the friend who does the dying, on purpose, for the ones he calls friends — and then he does not stay dead. He is the friend who sticks closer than a brother in the most literal, costly, permanent way history has ever recorded, and the sticking did not end at a graveside. It continues.

That changes what this verse is for. It is not only a warning to choose your circle carefully, although it is that. It is an invitation to notice who has already been sticking close to you, and to grow grateful rather than casual about them. And for anyone who feels they have never had a friend like that, it is a quiet promise that such a friend exists — and has already offered himself.

So what do you do with a verse like this on an ordinary Monday? Start small. Think of the one or two people who have already proven they stick — not the biggest group chat, not the most frequent texter, but the one who stayed when staying was inconvenient. Call that person today, not to catch up, but simply to say thank you for not leaving. Say it plainly. Most people who stick close have never once been told what that cost them.

Then consider the other side of the verse. Somewhere near you is a person surrounded by companions but genuinely alone — rich in acquaintances and starved for anyone who actually stays. You do not need a grand gesture to become that friend. You need to be the one who still calls after the crowd has moved on to the next thing. A thousand acquaintances can applaud a person. Only a friend stays when there is nothing left to applaud.

And if today you cannot think of anyone who has stuck that close, take the proverb as more than ancient advice. Take it as an open door. The friend Solomon describes has a name — and he has already said yes to you, before you ever asked.
